  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">One Model, Many Latencies: Universal Speech Enhancement for
Diverse Real-Time Applications
</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Szu-Wei Fu<sup id="id1" class="ltx_sup">1</sup>,
Rong Chao<sup id="id2" class="ltx_sup">2</sup>,
Xuesong Yang<sup id="id3" class="ltx_sup">1</sup>,
Sung-Feng Huang<sup id="id4" class="ltx_sup">1</sup>, 
<br class="ltx_break">Ante Jukić<sup id="id5" class="ltx_sup">1</sup>,
Yu Tsao<sup id="id6" class="ltx_sup">2</sup>,
Yu-Chiang Frank Wang<sup id="id7" class="ltx_sup">1</sup>
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span><sup id="id8" class="ltx_sup">1</sup>NVIDIA
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span><sup id="id9" class="ltx_sup">2</sup>Academia Sinica, Taipei, Taiwan
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Different real-time speech applications impose distinct latency budgets, often requiring separately trained enhancement models for each scenario. In this paper, we propose a one-for-all, real-time universal speech enhancement model that provides explicit control over both algorithmic and computational latency. Algorithmic latency is flexibly adjusted via configurable look-ahead frames. To avoid learning inefficiency caused by varying padding configurations, we introduce parallel convolutional layers corresponding to different look-ahead settings. Computational latency is controlled through an early-exit mechanism, enabling inference at different network depths. To narrow the performance gap between specialized and flexible models, we propose a two-stage training strategy with a shared-to-multiple decoder transition. Overall, the proposed framework enables a single model to be deployed across diverse latency budgets without retraining separate models. Model weights are available for download at: <a href="https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Real-time_RE-USE" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Real-time_RE-USE</a></p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Index Terms: </h6>universal speech enhancement, real-time processing, latency budget

</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">I </span><span id="S1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Introduction</span></h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recent studies in speech enhancement (SE) have increasingly moved beyond task-specific approaches toward unified models that generalize across heterogeneous domains <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>, <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>. In this context, universal speech enhancement (USE) seeks to improve intelligibility and perceptual quality under diverse degradation conditions while preserving intrinsic attributes such as speaker identity, emotion, and accent. Although Miipher-2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>, and RE-USE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>
have demonstrated effectiveness in improving training data quality for other speech generative models (e.g., text-to-speech), their non-causal architectures limit their applicability to real-time scenarios.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The total latency of a real-time speech
enhancement model is the <span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">sum of algorithmic latency and computational latency</span>, as illustrated in Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Fig. 1 ‣ I Introduction ‣ One Model, Many Latencies: Universal Speech Enhancement for Diverse Real-Time Applications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. Algorithmic latency refers to the amount of input required by the model to produce the first output unit. For frequency-domain–based USE models, the <span id="S1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">algorithmic latency equals the STFT window size <math id="S1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>w</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w</annotation></semantics></math> plus the product of the look-ahead frames and the hop size <math id="S1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math></span>. Computational latency denotes the time required by the model to generate an output after receiving the necessary input data, and <span id="S1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">it depends on both model complexity and the computational capability of the deployment hardware</span>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.25621v3/latency_def3.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/286;" width="476" height="286" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fig. 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">The latency of a speech enhancement system can be categorized into algorithmic latency and computational latency.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Unlike the restoration of pre-recorded speech, which prioritizes output quality over latency constraints, real-time speech enhancement must operate under strict latency budgets. These constraints vary across applications: interactive speech applications such as conversational VoIP typically tolerate 50–150 ms <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>, while streaming ASR systems generally operate within latency budgets of 100–200 ms <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>. Beyond different latency budget considerations, computational latency is influenced by the computational power of the deployment hardware (see Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Fig. 1 ‣ I Introduction ‣ One Model, Many Latencies: Universal Speech Enhancement for Diverse Real-Time Applications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>). <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">These factors prevent a single causal model from being suitable across different applications.</span> Accordingly, this paper aims to develop a training method that allows a single model to accommodate varying deployment conditions, such as latency constraints and hardware specifications.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To enable a single streaming ASR model to support various latency settings, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite> proposed a multiple look-ahead training strategy by randomly sampling the chunk size.
An effective strategy for reducing computational latency is early exit <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>, a training paradigm that enables a network to produce predictions at intermediate layers rather than only at the final layer, allowing the model to seamlessly adapt to different deployment conditions during inference. In the context of speech enhancement, several studies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>, <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite> have adopted early-exit mechanisms to build flexible models. Nevertheless, most of them focus primarily on designing the exit criteria. For example, Li et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite> and Chen et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite> explored exit strategies based on the similarity between outputs of consecutive layers, using predefined thresholds to determine when to exit. Beyond dynamically adjusting the model depth, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite> introduces FlexAttention to enable flexible control over model width.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Although early-exit can adjust computational latency during inference, algorithmic latency remains fixed. In this paper, we propose a <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">one-for-all</span>, real-time, streamable USE model that not only handles diverse degradation conditions but also provides explicit control over algorithmic latency via flexible look-ahead frames, thereby enabling adaptable total latency and facilitating deployment across a wide range of latency budgets.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">II </span><span id="S2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">From Offline to Real-Time Speech Enhancement</span></h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Before presenting our proposed method, this section outlines the constraints that a real-time SE model must satisfy, based on the total latency definition illustrated in Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Fig. 1 ‣ I Introduction ‣ One Model, Many Latencies: Universal Speech Enhancement for Diverse Real-Time Applications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. Some of these constraints are often overlooked in prior studies. Specifically, real-time SE models must meet the following three requirements:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">1. <span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Causality</span>: The model architecture should be causal or allow only a limited number of look-ahead frames.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">2. <span id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Latency budget</span> (<math id="S2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l_{\text{budget}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>l</mi><mtext>budget</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l_{\text{budget}}</annotation></semantics></math>): The total latency must not exceed the application-specific latency budget (examples are discussed in Section <a href="#S1" title="I Introduction ‣ One Model, Many Latencies: Universal Speech Enhancement for Diverse Real-Time Applications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a>):</p>
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l_{\text{Total}}\leq l_{\text{budget}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>l</mi><mtext>Total</mtext></msub><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>l</mi><mtext>budget</mtext></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l_{\text{Total}}\leq l_{\text{budget}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">3. <span id="S2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Real-time processing</span>: To prevent latency from accumulating over time, the computation time per processing step must be shorter than the corresponding hop size <math id="S2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> (i.e., the real-time factor (RTF) must be less than 1):</p>
<table id="S2.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l_{\text{Compute}}\leq h." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>l</mi><mtext>Compute</mtext></msub><mo>≤</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l_{\text{Compute}}\leq h.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">As noted by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>, some prior studies may report RTF measured under offline processing, where whole utterances are processed at once. This setting exploits time-dimension parallelism and highly optimized large-tensor CUDA kernels, and thus can substantially underestimate the true RTF in streaming inference, obscuring whether a method is practically real-time.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">III </span><span id="S3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Proposed Method</span></h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S3.SS1.6" class="ltx_text">III-A</span> </span><span id="S3.SS1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Adjustable Algorithmic Latency</span></h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To enable adjustable algorithmic latency during inference, it is more practical to control the number of look-ahead frames rather than modifying the STFT window size or hop length. In practice, the number of look-ahead frames can be determined by appropriately setting the left and right padding of the convolutional layers. For example, consider a convolutional layer with a kernel size of 3. To achieve 0, 1, and 2 look-ahead frames, the (left padding, right padding) number can be set to (2, 0), (1, 1), and (0, 2), respectively. However, since convolution is <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">translation equivariant</span> (i.e., if <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> is a convolution operation and <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> is a translation (shift) operator: <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f(T(x))=T(f(x))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(T(x))=T(f(x))</annotation></semantics></math>), using a single convolutional layer with varying padding configurations may disrupt the following sequence modeling and thereby reduce the model’s learning efficiency (see the green learning curve corresponding to the UTMOS score on the validation set in Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Fig. 3 ‣ III-A Adjustable Algorithmic Latency ‣ III Proposed Method ‣ One Model, Many Latencies: Universal Speech Enhancement for Diverse Real-Time Applications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. Detailed experimental settings are provided in Section <a href="#S4" title="IV Experiments ‣ One Model, Many Latencies: Universal Speech Enhancement for Diverse Real-Time Applications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">IV</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To address this issue, inspired by the mixture-of-experts (MoE) paradigm, we employ parallel convolutional layers, each corresponding to a specific number of look-ahead frames (i.e., a particular padding configuration). During training, a convolutional layer is randomly sampled to construct the computational graph. Unlike conventional MoE models, our framework does not require a learned routing mechanism, as the expert selection is explicitly determined by the user based on the latency budget, as illustrated in Fig. <a href="#S3.F2" title="Fig. 2 ‣ III-A Adjustable Algorithmic Latency ‣ III Proposed Method ‣ One Model, Many Latencies: Universal Speech Enhancement for Diverse Real-Time Applications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2606.25621v3/proposed_model3.png" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/476;" width="476" height="476" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fig. 2</span>: </span><span id="S3.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Our proposed one-for-all model enables adjustable algorithmic latency through configurable look-ahead frames and computational latency via early exit. For example, under a low-latency budget, inference can follow the orange arrows.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2606.25621v3/Learnining_curves.svg" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/259;" width="476" height="259"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Fig. 3</span>: </span><span id="S3.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Learning curves of UTMOS scores on the validation set under different model architectures.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S3.SS2.6" class="ltx_text">III-B</span> </span><span id="S3.SS2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Two-Stage Training for Early-Exit Optimization</span></h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Although the early-exit mechanism enables flexible inference at different network depths, each intermediate layer represents a compromise, as it must accommodate the requirements of subsequent layers. Consequently, its performance lags behind that of a model optimized for a fixed output depth. One possible remedy is to assign separate decoders to different intermediate layers. However, in the initial experiments on early-exit training, we found that <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">sharing a single decoder across all intermediate layers</span> is more effective, as it enforces a consistent representation space. In contrast, using independent decoders for each layer hinders model learning, as shown in the blue line in Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Fig. 3 ‣ III-A Adjustable Algorithmic Latency ‣ III Proposed Method ‣ One Model, Many Latencies: Universal Speech Enhancement for Diverse Real-Time Applications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To address this issue and allow each output layer to learn layer-specific parameters, we adopt a two-stage training framework:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<ol id="S3.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Shared Decoder Stage:</span> We first train the model with a shared decoder. In each training step, the exit layers are randomly sampled.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Multiple Decoder Stage:</span> After convergence in the first stage, we instantiate independent decoders for each output layer, <span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">initializing their weights from the shared decoder</span>. During this stage, the modules preceding the decoders (i.e., the encoder and sequence modeling module) are fine-tuned with a smaller learning rate.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">This setting keeps the intermediate layers within a similar representation space while allowing sufficient flexibility to optimize their own outputs.</span></p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">IV </span><span id="S4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Experiments</span></h2>

<figure id="S4.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">TABLE I</span>: </span><span id="S4.T1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Non-blind test set results of the URGENT 2025 Challenge. Algo. and Comp. denote algorithmic and computational latency, respectively. Algorithmic latency is computed as <math id="S4.T1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="40\,\mathrm{ms}+(\#\,\text{look\mbox{-}ahead}\times 20\,\mathrm{ms})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>40</mn><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ms</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathsize="1.110em">#</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mtext>look</mtext><mtext>-</mtext><mtext>ahead</mtext></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ms</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">40\,\mathrm{ms}+(\#\,\text{look\mbox{-}ahead}\times 20\,\mathrm{ms})</annotation></semantics></math>. Computational latency is evaluated on an NVIDIA A100 GPU with 16 kHz input speech.
</span></figcaption>
<div id="S4.T1.5" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:341.6pt;height:301.6pt;vertical-align:-149.5pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-155.6pt,137.4pt) scale(0.523189379079918,0.523189379079918) ;">
<table id="S4.T1.5.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="S4.T1.5.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T1.5.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt" style="padding-top:-0.3pt;padding-bottom:-0.3pt;"><span id="S4.T1.5.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Method</span></td>
<td id="S4.T1.5.1.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt" style="padding-top:-0.3pt;padding-bottom:-0.3pt;" colspan="3"><span id="S4.T1.5.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Non-intrusive</span></td>

<td id="S4.T1.5.1.23.8" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding-top:-0.3pt;padding-bottom:-0.3pt;">0.77</td>

</figure>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS1.6" class="ltx_text">IV-A</span> </span><span id="S4.SS1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Dataset</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Following the setup of the URGENT 2025 Challenge <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite>, the training dataset consists of multi-condition speech recordings in five languages (English, German, French, Spanish, and Chinese), covering a wide range of sampling rates (8, 16, 22.05, 24, 32, 44.1, and 48 kHz). In addition to clean speech, the dataset includes noise samples and room impulse responses (RIRs). Seven types of degradations are considered: additive noise, reverberation, clipping, bandwidth limitation, codec artifacts, packet loss, and wind noise. The validation set is simulated according to the organizers’ guidelines using the validation splits of the underlying corpora <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>]</cite>.
The final model checkpoint is selected based on the UTMOS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite> score on the validation set. For evaluation, we use the non-blind URGENT 2025 test set, which contains 1,000 utterances.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS2.6" class="ltx_text">IV-B</span> </span><span id="S4.SS2.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Model Architecture</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our model architecture largely follows USEMamba <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite> and RE-USE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>, as Mamba <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite> supports RNN-like inference and hence is well-suited for real-time deployment. Considering computational latency constraints, we set the maximum number of Mamba layers to 12 (total 3.7M parameters). To ensure causality or allow only a limited number of look-ahead frames, we introduce the following modifications: (1) replacing standard convolutions with causal convolutions (we explicitly control the number of look-ahead frames by using different amounts of left padding in the first convolutional layer); (2) substituting the bidirectional temporal Mamba with a unidirectional variant; and (3) replacing instance normalization with layer normalization applied only along the channel dimension.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Unlike RE-USE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>, which employs an additional generative model to refine the regression output and achieve a favorable fidelity–quality trade-off, we reduce computational latency by approximating the process of ‘optimally transporting the posterior mean (MMSE estimate) toward the true data distribution’ through a two-stage training strategy: regression loss pre-training followed by adversarial loss fine-tuning guided by a set of discriminators.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To enable a single model to operate across different sampling rates, we adopt sampling frequency-independent (SFI) STFT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>, which adjusts the FFT window and hop size according to the input sampling rate while maintaining a fixed time duration. Specifically, we use a 40 ms window and a 20 ms hop for all sampling rates, ensuring an integer number of frequency bins. Therefore, the resulting <span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">algorithmic latency is 40 ms plus the number of look-ahead frames multiplied by 20 ms</span>. During training, we randomly sample the exit layer from 3 to 12 and the number of look-ahead frames from 0 to 2.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We use AdamW with a learning rate of 0.0002 for model training, and set the learning rate to one-tenth of this value for the modules preceding the decoders during the Multiple Decoder Stage.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS3.6" class="ltx_text">IV-C</span> </span><span id="S4.SS3.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Evaluation Metrics</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To jointly assess perceptual quality and signal fidelity, we employ a diverse set of evaluation metrics. Reference-based metrics include PESQ for perceptual quality <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite>, ESTOI for intelligibility <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>. Downstream performance is evaluated using task-independent metrics—SpeechBERTScore (SBERT) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite> and Levenshtein Phoneme Similarity (LPS) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite>—as well as task-dependent metrics, character accuracy (CAcc) of an ASR  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>. Finally, non-intrusive perceptual quality is measured using DNSMOS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite>, NISQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>]</cite>, and UTMOS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>. Note that, following the setup in RE-USE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>, we compute the scores using anechoic clean speech as the reference, rather than early-reflected speech as adopted by the Challenge organizers.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For latency calculation, algorithmic latency is computed as <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="40\,\mathrm{ms}+(\#\,\text{look\mbox{-}ahead}\times 20\,\mathrm{ms})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>40</mn><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ms</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>#</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mtext>look</mtext><mtext>-</mtext><mtext>ahead</mtext></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>ms</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">40\,\mathrm{ms}+(\#\,\text{look\mbox{-}ahead}\times 20\,\mathrm{ms})</annotation></semantics></math>, while computational latency is evaluated on an NVIDIA A100 GPU using 16 kHz input speech. We also evaluated the latency on NVIDIA 3090 and 4090 GPUs and observed results within a similar range. Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>, computational latency is measured under online processing (i.e., per-frame computation). However, unlike <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>, we do not apply <span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">torch.compile</span> or CUDA graphs to further optimize latency measurement.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS4.6" class="ltx_text">IV-D</span> </span><span id="S4.SS4.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Results on the non-Blind URGENT 2025 Test Set</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Owing to the flexibility of our proposed one-for-all framework in controlling both algorithmic and computational latency, the model supports 30 different latency configurations, corresponding to 10 exit layers (from 3 to 12) and 3 look-ahead settings (from 0 to 2). In Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="TABLE I ‣ IV Experiments ‣ One Model, Many Latencies: Universal Speech Enhancement for Diverse Real-Time Applications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a>, we present representative results of our method and compare them with noisy speech, the non-causal baseline TF-GridNet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite> from the URGENT 2025 Challenge (which uses early-reflected speech as the learning target), as well as specialized models and early-exit. The specialized model can be regarded as a performance upper bound, but does not provide any latency flexibility. Note that for the 12-layer model, the computational latency is 25 ms, which exceeds the hop size of 20 ms, resulting in an RTF of 1.25. This means it cannot satisfy real-time processing requirements (see Section <a href="#S2" title="II From Offline to Real-Time Speech Enhancement ‣ One Model, Many Latencies: Universal Speech Enhancement for Diverse Real-Time Applications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">II</span></a>) on an NVIDIA A100 GPU, and <span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">a faster GPU would be needed to achieve real-time performance.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="TABLE I ‣ IV Experiments ‣ One Model, Many Latencies: Universal Speech Enhancement for Diverse Real-Time Applications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a> and discussed in Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="III-B Two-Stage Training for Early-Exit Optimization ‣ III Proposed Method ‣ One Model, Many Latencies: Universal Speech Enhancement for Diverse Real-Time Applications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">III-B</span></a>, while early-exit enables flexible control of computational latency, its enhancement performance typically falls short of the specialized model. Our proposed method (<span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Parallel conv. (MoE)</span>), which introduces parallel convolutional layers to control the number of look-ahead frames, achieves performance comparable to early-exit while additionally providing flexibility in controlling algorithmic latency. The proposed two-stage training framework (<span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Multiple dec. stage</span>), incorporating the multiple-decoder stage, consistently improves most evaluation metrics—most notably CAcc (with the exception of NISQA)—and effectively narrows the performance gap with the specialized model.
<span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Note that the results for the conventional early-exit model with (Exit Layer = 8, Look-ahead = 1) are marked as N/A, since the conventional early-exit method does not support adjusting the algorithmic latency.</span></p>
</div>

</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In Fig. <a href="#S4.F4" title="Fig. 4 ‣ IV-D Results on the non-Blind URGENT 2025 Test Set ‣ IV Experiments ‣ One Model, Many Latencies: Universal Speech Enhancement for Diverse Real-Time Applications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, we present performance evaluation over a finer grid of total latency. Note that our one-for-all model supports 30 distinct latency configurations; results for exit layers 3, 5, 7, 9, and 11 are omitted for brevity. From the figure, we observe that for UTMOS, performance gains from additional look-ahead frames are less pronounced than those achieved by increasing the model depth. On the other hand, for ASR accuracy, introducing one look-ahead frame substantially improves performance, while adding a second look-ahead frame yields only marginal additional gains.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS5.6" class="ltx_text">IV-E</span> </span><span id="S4.SS5.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Comparison with Other Real-Time Speech Enhancement Models</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">To the best of our knowledge, no prior open-source work has proposed a real-time universal speech enhancement model capable of handling complex degradations and inputs with varying sampling rates, as required in the URGENT Challenge setting</span>. Therefore, to enable comparison with existing real-time speech enhancement models, we evaluate our approach on the widely used VoiceBank-DEMAND benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite>, as shown in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="TABLE II ‣ IV-D Results on the non-Blind URGENT 2025 Test Set ‣ IV Experiments ‣ One Model, Many Latencies: Universal Speech Enhancement for Diverse Real-Time Applications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">II</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For the baselines and to evaluate generalization across datasets, we use DEMUCS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>, DeepFilterNet3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite>, Diffusion Buffer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite>, and Stream.FM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>, with most results directly taken from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>. Note that, <span id="S4.SS5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">consistent with our setting, there is a mismatch between the training and testing data, as none of the compared models (except DEMUCS) are trained on the VoiceBank-DEMAND training set</span>. For our proposed model, we first set the exit layer to 8 and the look-ahead to 0 to achieve a comparable algorithmic latency to DEMUCS, DeepFilterNet3, and Stream.FM. Compared with these models, our method achieves the highest PESQ, ESTOI, and SI-SDR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>. We also observe that the enhanced speech produced by our model often sounds cleaner than the corresponding clean ground truth.
In our model, setting the look-ahead to 1 increases the algorithmic latency but consistently improves all evaluation metrics, demonstrating the flexibility of our framework.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection"><span id="S4.SS6.6" class="ltx_text">IV-F</span> </span><span id="S4.SS6.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Practical Deployment</span></h3>

<div id="S4.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Users can download the model and evaluate the total latency across different early-exit layers and look-ahead configurations on their own hardware, according to their specific latency budgets. Once the most suitable setting is identified, they can retain only the layers up to the selected exit point and the convolutional branch corresponding to the chosen look-ahead frames. In this way, the resulting model has the same size as a specialized model, without any additional footprint.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Note that computational latency must satisfy the constraints in both Equations (<a href="#S2.E1" title="In II From Offline to Real-Time Speech Enhancement ‣ One Model, Many Latencies: Universal Speech Enhancement for Diverse Real-Time Applications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) and (<a href="#S2.E2" title="In II From Offline to Real-Time Speech Enhancement ‣ One Model, Many Latencies: Universal Speech Enhancement for Diverse Real-Time Applications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>), whereas algorithmic latency is governed only by Equation (<a href="#S2.E1" title="In II From Offline to Real-Time Speech Enhancement ‣ One Model, Many Latencies: Universal Speech Enhancement for Diverse Real-Time Applications" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>). Therefore, if users have limited computational resources, they can simply consider increasing the number of look-ahead frames.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">V </span><span id="S5.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Future work</span></h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we focus on training a flexible one-for-all model that can be readily deployed under diverse conditions. Techniques such as pruning and quantization offer promising directions for accelerating inference and can be naturally combined with our framework. Another avenue for future work is to further reduce the performance gap between shallow and deep outputs. In particular, knowledge distillation strategies, inspired by recent large-to-small language model compression, may be explored to enhance the performance of shallower exits.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">VI </span><span id="S6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Conclusion</span></h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose a one-for-all, real-time universal speech enhancement framework that explicitly controls both algorithmic and computational latency within a single model. By introducing parallel convolutional layers, we enable flexible adjustment of look-ahead frames for algorithmic latency control, while the early-exit mechanism allows dynamic control of computational latency through variable network depth. To mitigate the performance gap between flexible and specialized models, we further developed a two-stage training strategy with a shared-to-multiple decoder transition, which effectively stabilizes learning and improves intermediate-layer performance. Experimental results on the URGENT 2025 Challenge dataset demonstrate that the proposed framework supports 30 distinct latency configurations while maintaining performance close to specialized models. These results show that a single model can adapt to diverse real-time applications without retraining separate models.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">VII </span><span id="S7.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">Generative AI Use Disclosure</span></h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Generative AI was used only for editing and polishing this manuscript.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
